newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: ING questions S&P Argentine corporate rating hikes.
newsitem.headline: ING questions S&P Argentine corporate rating hikes.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp's upgrade of the foreign currency credit ratings of several Argentine corporations has raised more questions than answers, ING Barings said in a report published Tuesday.
ING's main point is that the change in the ratings criteria by the McGraw-Hill Cos Inc unit as a result of the dollarization of Argentina's economy should be applied to the sovereign rating as well.

"To the extent that dollarization is a determinant of creditworthiness, it is a criterion that should be applied first and foremost to the sovereign -- not, as in this case, to corporates alone," said Arturo Porzecanski, ING Barings Americas chief economist in the report.
Dollarization is the process by which the dollar or another hard currency becomes the main store of value in a country.

S&P raised the ratings on several corporates because it considers that the level of dollarization in Argentina has reached a point where it is very unlikely the government will interfere with private sector foreign exchange transactions, "even in a scenario involving sovereign default."

ING said this argument can just as easily be applied to Argentina's sovereign rating because the "government can tap a sizeable pool of dollars in the hands of individuals, banks and corporations that did not exist or was beyond the reach of the authorities in previous decades."
One example of Argentines' increased holding of dollars is their purchases of dollar-denominated treasury bills and bonds.

ING also questioned S&P's reasoning in comparing the dollarization of Panama's economy with that of Argentina's. The central role of the dollar in Panama's economy was enshrined in the country's constitution in 1903.
Panama has no central bank and has a history of nearly 100 years of not imposing limits on the transfer of dollars, even during the 1980s, when the government itself fell into arrears.
"Argentina, on the other hand, has experienced creeping dollarization as a result of a legacy of unsound policies leading to frequent episodes of hyperinflation and capital flight," said ING.

Argentina has a central bank which has several times resorted to printing currency, introduced foreign exchange regimes, frozen financial assets and imposed restrictions on payments including those made by the private sector to abroad.
"In sum, Argentina has not been, and is not becoming, another Panama," said ING.

ING questioned S&P's decision to raise the ratings on Argentine banks to above the sovereign credit rating ceiling as well. It argues that as these banks operate under the control of the Argentine central bank, which is a sovereign body, they should not be rated above the sovereign.

The obvious way in which banks' "ability to service foreign-currency obligations is not independent of the sovereign" is the way in which the central bank sets reserve and liquidity requirements. "This is true in Argentina as it is in most countries - dollarized or not."

All the same, "we believe that several of the companies deserved to receive an investment-grade rating based on their foreign revenues or strong support from foreign shareholders. As concerns several other companies - purely domestic utilities and banks - we find the upgrade more difficult to defend," said ING.
Firms' foreign currency debt ratings which were raised to BBB- (the lowest investment-grade) include Astra SA, Edesur, Perez Companc SA, YPF SA and Transportadora de Gas del Norte.
Financial institutions that were raise to BBB- were Banco Rio de la Plata, Banco Frances del Rio de la Plata and Caja de Valores SA.
Argentina's sovereign foreign currency debt rating is BB.
